title: GMAT Focus Verbal Practice Test 27
instructions: Original exam-style practice test with answers and explanations.

questions.prompt: A nursery school introduced a daily outdoor session and reports that children nap more readily in the afternoon. The head concludes that outdoor activity improves children's sleep.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. The outdoor session lasts an hour.
B. Some children do not nap at all.
C. The session replaced a period of quiet indoor play that had been scheduled immediately before the nap, and children had often been unsettled by the transition from it.
D. Staff supervise the session in pairs.
E. The nursery has a large garden.
questions.explanation: What changed may be the removal of an unsettling transition rather than the addition of activity, and the two are confounded in a single schedule change.

questions.prompt: An ice rink introduced an online booking system and reports that its sessions now sell out more often. The manager concludes that demand for skating has risen.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously undermines the conclusion?
options: A. Booking online requires an account.
B. Sessions last ninety minutes.
C. Some customers still pay at the door.
D. The rink is open year-round.
E. The rink reduced the number of skaters admitted to each session at the same time, on safety advice.
questions.explanation: A smaller capacity produces more sell-outs at unchanged demand, so the indicator moved for a reason unrelated to interest in skating.

questions.prompt: A vineyard reports that its wines score higher in competitions in years when it harvests late, and plans to harvest late every year.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, casts most doubt on the plan?
options: A. Late harvesting requires additional labour.
B. The vineyard harvests late only when the autumn weather is settled, and picks early in years when rain threatens the crop.
C. Competition judges taste blind.
D. The vineyard produces both red and white wines.
E. Some competitions award medals in several classes.
questions.explanation: The harvest date is chosen in response to the conditions that themselves determine quality, so the association cannot be converted into a rule.

questions.prompt: A coach operator introduced reclining seats on its long-distance routes and reports that customer satisfaction scores rose. It plans to fit them on its city routes to raise satisfaction there.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the plan?
options: A. Reclining seats are heavier than standard ones.
B. The seats are more expensive to maintain.
C. Some long-distance passengers travel overnight.
D. City journeys average eighteen minutes, and complaints on those routes concern frequency and reliability rather than comfort.
E. Satisfaction is measured by an online survey.
questions.explanation: The remedy addresses a constraint that does not bind on short journeys, so the same intervention should not be expected to transfer.

questions.prompt: Every policy sold by the Greenway pet insurer that covers dental treatment requires an annual check-up. No policy requiring an annual check-up has been cancelled for non-disclosure this year. Some Greenway policies have been cancelled for non-disclosure this year.
questions.question: If the statements above are true, which of the following must be true?
options: A. Some Greenway policies do not cover dental treatment.
B. Annual check-ups prevent non-disclosure.
C. Most policies cover dental treatment.
D. Dental cover is more expensive.
E. Policies without check-ups are sold to older animals.
questions.explanation: Cancelled policies do not require a check-up, and dental cover implies one, so those policies carry no dental cover.

questions.prompt: A community centre began charging a small fee for its evening classes and reports that attendance at each class is now more consistent, with fewer people booking and not arriving. The manager concludes that people value what they pay for.
questions.question: Which of the following would be most useful to determine in evaluating the conclusion?
options: A. How the fee compares with fees at other centres
B. Whether classes are held on weekdays
C. Whether the number of people booking classes fell after the fee was introduced
D. How many classes the centre offers
E. Whether tutors are paid per session
questions.explanation: Consistency could rise because the fee deterred marginal bookers rather than because it changed anyone's valuation; the booking figure distinguishes the two.

questions.prompt: A sawmill installed a scanner that measures each log and calculates the most valuable cutting pattern. It reports that the value of timber produced per log rose by 9 per cent, and concludes that the scanner has paid for itself.
questions.question: The conclusion depends on which of the following assumptions?
options: A. Operators trust the scanner's recommendations.
B. The additional value produced exceeds the cost of the scanner and its operation over the relevant period.
C. Logs arrive at the mill in similar sizes.
D. The mill processes hardwood as well as softwood.
E. Timber prices did not fall during the period.
questions.explanation: Paying for itself is a claim about net cost, not about output value; the yield gain alone cannot establish it. E affects the size of the gain but not the structure of the inference.

questions.prompt: A tool hire firm reports that customers who take out its damage waiver return equipment in better condition than those who decline it, and concludes that the waiver encourages careful handling.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the conclusion?
options: A. Trade customers, who handle tools professionally, take the waiver as a matter of routine, while occasional domestic hirers decline it to save money.
B. The waiver costs a small percentage of the hire fee.
C. Damage is assessed on return by staff.
D. The firm hires out both hand and power tools.
E. Some customers hire the same tool repeatedly.
questions.explanation: Skill, not the waiver, distinguishes the groups, and the waiver would if anything reduce the incentive to be careful.

questions.prompt: A fish market reports that stalls trading before seven in the morning sell more per stall than those opening later, and advises all stallholders to open earlier.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the advice?
options: A. Some stalls sell shellfish only.
B. The market opens at five.
C. Later stalls serve mainly household shoppers.
D. The early stalls are those supplying restaurants under standing orders placed the previous day, and those orders would not increase if other stalls opened earlier.
E. Stall rents are the same throughout the day.
questions.explanation: The sales difference comes from a contracted trade that opening hours cannot transfer, so the advice mistakes a customer type for a schedule effect.

questions.prompt: A bus depot introduced a maintenance regime based on mileage rather than a fixed calendar and reports that breakdowns fell by a fifth. Managers conclude that mileage is a better basis for scheduling maintenance.
questions.question: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the conclusion?
options: A. The new regime required additional record-keeping.
B. Mechanics preferred the new system.
C. The depot also replaced four older vehicles.
D. Breakdowns are recorded by drivers.
E. A second depot that kept the calendar regime over the same period, using the same vehicle types on similar routes, recorded no change in breakdowns.
questions.explanation: A matched depot on the old regime supplies the comparison; D introduces a rival explanation for the same fall.

questions.prompt: An optician reports that customers who buy anti-reflective lens coatings report fewer headaches than those who do not, and advertises the coating as reducing headaches.
questions.question: The advertisement is most vulnerable to the criticism that it
options: A. does not specify how headaches were measured
B. ignores the cost of the coating
C. assumes a difference between self-selecting customers was produced by the coating
D. relies on reports made some months after purchase
E. overlooks customers who wear contact lenses
questions.explanation: Customers who buy an upgrade sold as reducing eye strain are those already suffering it and expecting relief, which is both a selection and an expectation problem.

questions.passageText:
A firm whose managers perform poorly should, in theory, become cheap enough that an outsider can buy it, replace them, and profit from the improvement. This threat is supposed to discipline managers who face no other effective supervision, and the argument is coherent. Whether the mechanism works as described is a different question.

Several things blunt it. A bidder must pay a premium over the market price, so the improvement must exceed both the premium and the cost of the bid before anything is gained. Managers can make a firm expensive to acquire through provisions that require a bidder to win a slow proxy contest, and those provisions are adopted by the very people the threat is meant to discipline. And the acquirer's own managers may be pursuing size rather than value, in which case the discipline runs in the wrong direction: a badly governed acquirer buying a badly governed target improves nothing.

The evidence is correspondingly mixed. Target shareholders reliably gain, which is not in dispute; acquirer shareholders on average gain little and often lose, which is difficult to reconcile with a mechanism that is supposed to reallocate assets to better managers. Studies of operating performance after acquisition find improvements in some samples and none in others, with the results depending heavily on how performance is measured and over what period.

The defensible summary is narrower than the theory. The threat of acquisition constrains the most extreme forms of managerial failure, particularly where a firm's assets are visibly worth more than its shares. It does not constrain the ordinary sort, and treating it as a general substitute for governance mistakes a blunt instrument for a precise one.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, one obstacle to the disciplinary effect of takeovers is that
options: A. target shareholders resist all bids
B. regulators prohibit hostile acquisitions
C. acquirers cannot replace managers
D. the improvement must exceed both the acquisition premium and the cost of the bid
E. share prices do not reflect managerial quality
questions.explanation: The premium is paid before anything is gained, which is the first of the three blunting factors listed.

questions.passageText:
A unit of measurement must be defined by something anyone can reproduce, and the history of the metric system is a sequence of retreats from objects toward constants.

The metre began as a fraction of the Earth's meridian, which was measured by survey and turned out to have been measured slightly wrong. The definition then moved to a platinum-iridium bar in a vault near Paris, which had the advantage of being stable and the disadvantage of being a single object: any laboratory needing the metre needed a copy, copies drift, and if the bar had been damaged the unit would have been damaged with it. In 1983 the metre was redefined in terms of the distance light travels in a specified fraction of a second, which fixed the speed of light by definition and made the metre reproducible in any laboratory with a suitable clock.

The kilogram resisted longest. It remained a physical cylinder until 2019, and comparisons showed the international prototype drifting relative to its own official copies by tens of micrograms over a century — a discrepancy that was unmeasurable in absolute terms, since the prototype was the kilogram and could not by definition be wrong.

The redefinition tied the kilogram to the Planck constant through an apparatus that balances mechanical against electrical power. What the change delivers is not greater accuracy for everyday weighing, which was never in question, but the removal of a dependence on a single artefact — and the general principle that a standard resting on one object is only as durable as that object.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the disadvantage of defining the metre by a metal bar was that
options: A. the bar was inaccurate when made
B. platinum expands unpredictably
C. the bar was inaccessible to French laboratories
D. it depended on a survey of the Earth
E. it was a single object, so copies were needed and could drift
questions.explanation: The passage also notes damage to the bar would have damaged the unit itself.

questions.passageText:
Paid leave for new parents is now standard in most wealthy countries, and the research on it has become precise enough to distinguish effects that were once discussed together.

Short and moderate leave — a few months — is associated with better outcomes on several measures: higher rates of breastfeeding, fewer maternal health problems, and mothers more likely to return to the employer they left, which preserves the value of the job match. Very long leave produces a different pattern. Beyond about a year, women's earnings and promotion prospects fall relative to comparable women taking less, because skills depreciate, contacts weaken, and employers form expectations about who will be absent.

That last channel is the reason the design of leave matters as much as its length. Where leave is available to either parent but taken almost entirely by mothers, the expectation attaches to women as a class, including those who take no leave at all. Countries that reserved a portion for fathers on a use-it-or-lose-it basis saw take-up by fathers rise substantially, which is the intended effect; the evidence that this has closed earnings gaps is weaker and slower to appear.

The honest position is that leave policy trades between objectives on different timescales. Time with an infant is valuable now; attachment to the labour market is valuable later; and an employer's expectations are shaped by aggregate behaviour rather than by any individual's choice. A policy can be well designed for one of these and poorly designed for the others, and most public argument treats the three as though they were one.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, leave beyond about a year is associated with
options: A. higher rates of breastfeeding
B. improved job matches
C. greater take-up by fathers
D. falling earnings and promotion prospects relative to women taking less
E. fewer maternal health problems
questions.explanation: Skill depreciation, weakened contacts and employer expectations are the mechanisms given.

questions.passageText:
The great eighteenth-century encyclopedias are usually remembered for their contents. Their more consequential feature was structural: they organised knowledge alphabetically rather than by subject, and the choice was not neutral.

A subject-ordered work embodies a claim about how knowledge is arranged — what belongs under what, which discipline governs which question — and readers encounter that hierarchy before they reach any fact. Alphabetical order abolishes it. Entries sit beside their neighbours by accident of spelling, and a reader can enter anywhere without accepting a scheme first. Contemporaries understood this and argued about it: the arrangement was attacked as fragmenting knowledge into disconnected pieces, and defended as freeing readers from an inherited order that was itself a doctrine.

The compilers found a compromise in cross-references, which let them reconstruct connections the alphabet had severed, and which could also be used mischievously — a reference from an orthodox article to a sceptical one made an argument that neither article stated. Some of the boldest content in these works lies in where the references point.

The device is now so ordinary that its significance is hard to see. But the modern habits of entering a body of knowledge at an arbitrary point, following a link rather than a syllabus, and assembling an understanding from fragments in an order nobody designed, all begin here — and the objection then raised, that such reading yields information without structure, is the same objection now made about the successors of these works.
questions.prompt: According to the passage, the consequential feature of the eighteenth-century encyclopedias was
options: A. the number of contributors they employed
B. the accuracy of their scientific articles
C. their alphabetical rather than subject-based organisation
D. their price
E. their use of illustrations
questions.explanation: The passage argues this choice was not neutral, since subject order embodies a claim about how knowledge is arranged.

A policy can be well designed for one of these and poorly designed for the others, and most public argument treats the three as though they were one.

readingPassages.title: Ordering All Knowledge
readingPassages.text:
The great eighteenth-century encyclopedias are usually remembered for their contents. Their more consequential feature was structural: they organised knowledge alphabetically rather than by subject, and the choice was not neutral.

A subject-ordered work embodies a claim about how knowledge is arranged — what belongs under what, which discipline governs which question — and readers encounter that hierarchy before they reach any fact. Alphabetical order abolishes it. Entries sit beside their neighbours by accident of spelling, and a reader can enter anywhere without accepting a scheme first. Contemporaries understood this and argued about it: the arrangement was attacked as fragmenting knowledge into disconnected pieces, and defended as freeing readers from an inherited order that was itself a doctrine.

The compilers found a compromise in cross-references, which let them reconstruct connections the alphabet had severed, and which could also be used mischievously — a reference from an orthodox article to a sceptical one made an argument that neither article stated. Some of the boldest content in these works lies in where the references point.

The device is now so ordinary that its significance is hard to see. But the modern habits of entering a body of knowledge at an arbitrary point, following a link rather than a syllabus, and assembling an understanding from fragments in an order nobody designed, all begin here — and the objection then raised, that such reading yields information without structure, is the same objection now made about the successors of these works.
